utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone, both in the courtroom and outside the courtroom assisting us. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-84-T, the Prosecutor versus Ramush Haradinaj et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Re, are you ready to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, before Mr. Re starts, I would like to remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you gave at the beginning of your testimony last Friday. Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: There are just several matters I wish to clarify from the questions Mr. Emmerson asked you yesterday, and I'll just ask you a few questions on that. Okay?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The first one is about your mother. Just so it's clear, what is your mother's year of birth?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, but I think 1930 or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Another thing I just wish to ask you about is yesterday Mr. Emmerson - it was at page 64 of the transcript - asked you about your mother saying the men who searched you before the incident on March the 24th, 1998, had found a gun on you. And you said: "How can my mother or anyone else on earth for that matter know anything about that except for myself? It wasn't just once that they actually physically frisked me during that time when they stopped me, they frisked me about five times." Just to ensure that the interpretation was entirely clear, the five times of frisking, are you referring only to that occasion when you were stopped, or are you saying there was another four occasions on which you were frisked?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOSLAV STOJANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that occasion that evening, that evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Those are my questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, the Bench has no further questions for you. This means that this concludes your evidence. It was really short this morning. I take it at least that the re-examination has not triggered any need for further questions by the Defence? I see nodding no three times. Mr. Stojanovic, you have been in court here now for the third day, you answered all questions put to you. The Chamber would like to thank you for coming far way and wish you a safe trip home again. Madam Usher, would you please escort Mr. Stojanovic out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for calling me and good-bye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, is the Prosecution ready to call its next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, the next witness will be Mr. Mijat Stojanovic. Mr. Di Fazio will take his witness and with him is another lawyer on our team, Ms. Romana Schweiger, who is sitting in court with us today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, welcome in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Before you give evidence, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require you to make a solemn declaration that you'll speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out to you by Madam Usher, and I'd like to invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Please be seated. I said "Witness," I do understand that your name is Mijat Stojanovic. Mr. Stojanovic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Di Fazio, who is counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Di Fazio, please proceed. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Examination by Mr. Di Fazio:

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Witness, I'd like to get some personal details from you, please. Could I have your full name, your date of birth, and your place of birth, please?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: My name is Mijat Stojanovic. I was born on the 29th of January, 1964, in Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And I'd like to get details of your family, your immediate family, your siblings and parents, and I would like to have the details as they existed in early 1998. So can you do it this way: Start with your mother and father, tell us their names, and then start with the siblings, brothers and sisters. Start with the oldest and end with the youngest.

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: My mother's name is Ljubica; my father's -- my brothers' name is Predrag, Dragoslav, Vlado; and my sister is Slavica, Nadica, Milica, and Dragica; and there's another brother by the name of Veselin.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Sorry, I missed your father's name, I think?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: My father's name is Drago, but he was deceased at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I see. Thank you very much. Quite right. Although you were born in Djakovica, I think you lived most of your early years in a small village called Dubrava. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, I was born in Djakovica, but I lived in Dubrava until the age of 17 or 18, the entire time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And I have one other question about your family, your extended family, do you have a cousin called Veselin Stijovic?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Veselin Stijovic, yes, that is my cousin, my aunt's son.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. And just for completion, is that on your mother's side or your father's side? Mother's sibling or father's sibling?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Mother's side.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And does he -- does he have a nickname?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Vesko.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And do you have a nickname?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, everybody in my family calls me Kika.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Can the witness be shown Exhibit P10, please; it's the map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, this takes a bit of time until you see it on your screen. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. And I wonder if the court officer would be so kind as to expand the -- it's really the bottom half and in the area to the -- yes, thanks, that's right. And just a bit more, if you could. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Have a look at that map. Can you see Dubrava on it?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. I don't think it's in dispute that it's -- in this case that it's to the north of a place called Gramocelj, correct, and just south of another place called Glodjane; correct? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. MR. DI FAZIO: Thanks. Now -- yes, thank you, that's even better. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How far is Dubrava from Glodjane?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Dubrava was adjacent to Glodjane. Ours was the last house in Dubrava, and the next property was already in Glodjane.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, I want to try and give the Trial Chamber a sense of that. If you stood in the centre of Dubrava and you walked to the centre of Glodjane, about how far would that be?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Maybe a kilometre and a half, maybe 2 kilometres. I can't really be very specific about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, we have a grid on the map, so we know that it's -- MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- square kilometres. Please proceed. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And the buildings between Dubrava and Glodjane, is there open land in between the two places or are there buildings, houses and farms and shops and so on, in between, all the way from Dubrava to Glodjane?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: No, there is open land and a few scattered houses, but mostly on arable land or meadows, but the village of Dubrava itself has this centre, and then there is the centre of the village of Glodjane. And in between them, there is open land, meadows, and maybe just a few houses here and there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you for that description. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you. I've finished with the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you go to school in the area, primary school?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Until the fifth grade I went to Djakovica, then I went to Rznic, and then I completed my secondary education in Decani.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All the while continuing to live in the village of Dubrava and going from there to school?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What was the name of the school in Rznic?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Petar Prlja.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you know a gentleman named Ramush Haradinaj?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How long have you known him?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Ever since I started in the fifth grade when I transferred to the school in Rznic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did he attend that elementary school, that Petar Prlja elementary school?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How did you get to school -- to that school?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Well, we mostly walked. At that time, there were just a few -- the bus service ran just a few times a day, so most of us students would just walk there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And on those occasions, did you see Ramush Haradinaj, the child of course?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did he have siblings?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, Daut who went to school with him, too, he was a bit younger. So at one stage, he started going with his brother to school, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you know his parents?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: I did know his father Hilmi. I didn't know his mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What did his father do when you were young and when you were a teenager?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, for a while he worked in a shop in Rznic. I don't know whether it was in this period or maybe a little bit later. I can't really be certain, I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. And did you go to the shop from time to time and buy things?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And did you ever see Mr. Ramush Haradinaj or any of his brothers close to or around the shop?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: I don't remember seeing them in the shop.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: From time to time, did you see Ramush Haradinaj around your village or in the -- not necessarily just in Dubrava, but in the villages around Dubrava, including Glodjane?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: I did see him in Glodjane, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you know where he lived?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes. For a while he lived in the village centre until they built their house close to our house.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I see. Where -- about when was that?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Well, I can't really remember when it was that this house was built.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, no, that's fair enough. I'm not asking for a precise date, but can you perhaps thinking back in terms of your life, was it when you were a child, a kid, or was it perhaps later when you were a teenager? Can you try and fix it by reference to --

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Well, thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters apologise, we didn't catch the last part of the answer. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Just give us your answer again, if you wouldn't mind.

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes. When I was a young man.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And how far away was the house, the Haradinaj house, from your place?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: 150 to 200 metres, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: After the house was constructed, did you ever see Ramush Haradinaj? In and around the house, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, yes, at the property, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And what about his father, Hilmi, and his brother Daut?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: I remember seeing Hilmi, and I can't recall seeing Daut. The reason why I remember seeing Hilmi is because I would sometimes mow their meadows.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In -- do you know if he had other brothers?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Well, he did have some younger brothers, but I don't know them well at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: You are asking about Hilmi's brothers? MR. DI FAZIO: Oh, I see. No, that could have led to some confusion. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm asking about Ramush Haradinaj's brothers, did he have any other brothers that you knew of, apart from Daut?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: I knew them by sight, but I don't know their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thanks. You -- how long did you continue to live in the area?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Well, I lived there until the age of 18 permanently, and then I went to Belgrade to study. I first went to do my national service, and then I went to Belgrade to study, but I came back home quite often. MR. DI FAZIO: Sorry, if Your Honours would just bear with me.

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In between the time that you left to go off and do your military service and move to Belgrade, did you go back to Dubrava from time to time?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Not occasionally. I would go there quite often.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And after you went -- had been to university -- I'm sorry, I -- I don't think you actually said this, but I don't think it's in -- there's no problem with this. You actually started university in Belgrade, didn't you, and didn't finish it. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, I never graduated.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. Okay. Now, after that period of time, did you continue to go back to Dubrava the same frequency?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How often every year would you say that you went back to Dubrava and how often would you stay there when you did go back?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Two or three times a year at least. I would sometimes stay for a week, sometimes over a weekend, sometimes I would spend my whole leave there and eventually I got a job. Every time I was on leave, I went back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. And did that pattern continue up until the first part of 1998?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, in between the time that you went to university and the first part of 1998, during which time you were going back from time to time, did you ever see Ramush Haradinaj?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: If you can recall specific incidents, please tell us; if you can't, make that clear. I'd like to know if you can recall any specific incidents or whether you simply have a memory of seeing him from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: We did see quite a bit of each other, but I can't remember that particular incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. When you saw each other, would you greet each other or would you just simply recognise the individual?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: I can't remember if we greeted each other or not, but I'm sure we would recognise each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And in that period of time that I'm talking about now, the period of time when you went to university in Belgrade and the period of the first part of 1998, did you also continue to see his father from time to time during these visits?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about Daut, did you see him from time to time during these visits?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like you now to focus on the first part of 1998 and tell the Trial Chamber what your situation was; that is, where were you living at the time and what was your job? Where did you go to work?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Back in 1995, I left Belgrade in May 1995, I think. I started working with my brother in Indjija. We made oxidised dye, we had a small shop. Most of my market was in Kosovo, that's where I sold most of our stuff; therefore, between 1995 and 1998, I was caught spending most of my time in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Which brother were you working -- which brother were you in business with?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Veselin.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And where is Indjija?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: In Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, I'm not a native English speaker. "Dye," is that a kind of -- to colour textiles or ... MR. DI FAZIO: I don't know, it's a paint -- I'm sorry, I'll ask the witness and get the details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Tell the Trial Chamber, what exactly is the stuff that you were making?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Oxidised dye. It's a sort of colour, paint, you use to white-wash houses, that sort of thing. It's industrial and it's used in the construction business mainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thanks for that clarification. Where were you living between 1995 and 1998?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: As I said a while ago, I would occasionally go to Belgrade or perhaps to Indjija, but I was spending most of my time in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. Okay. And where precisely in Kosovo? And I'm really interested in where you were domiciled, where you were actually living, where you would go home to eat and sleep and so on, where is that?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Dubrava, Dubrava itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In the same home in which you had grown up in?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, the only home we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. Turn your mind now to the first two or three -- to the first three months of 1998, January, February, and March of 1998. I want to ask you about events in Dubrava. Firstly, did this pattern that you described to the Trial Chamber continue? Were you spending time in Dubrava in those three months?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes. Sometimes, of course, I would need to go out and try to sell some of our merchandise.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: But were they extended business trips, or did you -- were they shortish trips, you would come back to Dubrava?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Those were day trips. Normally, I would set out in the morning, I would go and tour a particular town in Kosovo, and be back home the same night.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. What sort of car did you drive?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: A Lada 1200, the Russian make, a station-wagon.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. And your brother Dragoslav, did he own a car; and if so, what make?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Dragoslav had two cars: A Mazda 626 and a Volkswagen, a Jetta.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. In the first two or three months of 1998, did you notice young men in the village of Dubrava?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: I did, everywhere in Dubrava and in Glodjane where their presence was even more conspicuous.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, young men are seen from towns and villages, of course. What I want to know is if there was anything unusual about the presence of these young men; in other words, different young men or in numbers that were different from your experience up until that time?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: There were many more of them, and I failed to recognise quite a few of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where would you see them exactly?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Normally, in the evening in the centres of those villages that I crossed on my way back.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Are you referring to Glodjane or other nearby villages as well?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Glodjane. I wasn't aware of the other neighbouring villages, with the exception of Glodjane and Dubrava.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you drive through Glodjane from time to time on the way to and from work or for other reasons in those first few months of 1998?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: There was an asphalt road through Glodjane, so that was the reason that I took that route most of the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber if you observed anything other than the mere presence of young men? Did you actually see them doing anything, or was there anything about them that attracted your attention, other than the fact that some of them were not from the area?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes. One evening I was on my way back home and I noticed that most of those young men were carrying bags.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What sort of bags?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: The Malboro kind, that sort of thing, the ones used for advertising.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm still not quite sure. What do you mean? Plastic bags? Plastic shopping bags? Or something else?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Plastic ones, plastic ones, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, why did that attract your attention? What was unusual about that?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: It was unusual that virtually each and every one of those young men should have a plastic bag like that. I was on my way back from wherever, I no longer remember, and as I passed through I realised that each and every one of those young men were carrying a plastic bag in their hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where were they -- were they apparently going somewhere, as far as from what you could discern?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: They were coming from over Dubrava way and heading for Glodjane.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Walking or in vehicles?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Walking, walking.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And in what sort of numbers?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: I can't say right now because they were walking quite far apart. There were quite many of them, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And was this a one-off episode, or is this a phenomenon that you saw on more than one occasion?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Just that evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And can you tell us when that was approximately in 1998? Now, if you can't, don't guess, but if you can give us an idea, please?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you ever get any information as to what was in the bags?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Sometime later, once I'd spoken to certain people whose names I can't exactly remember, I learned that inside those plastic bags they were carrying grenades.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Well, I'd like you now to tell the Trial Chamber as much as you can about the source of the information that you received, who you got the information from. I know you say you can't remember the names, but I want to know the ethnicity of the people, whether they were men or women, which village they were from, if there was more than one person who gave you the information. So tell the Trial Chamber as much as you can about your source of information about these bombs or grenades being in the bags.

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: I lived in an area where my home was the only Serb home, so the only people I could possibly have learned this from were the Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And can you remember if they volunteered the information to you about the bombs in the bags, or did you go out looking for information?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: I think I was the one who asked them. It was more of an informal contact or conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And from what you could see, were the young men carrying these bags going anywhere specific? I know you've told us that you saw, I think, Dubrava to -- Dubrava towards Glodjane, I think your evidence was, but did you see where they were going specifically?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: I don't know. They were going towards Glodjane, but there were many people who lived in Glodjane in the centre of that village. MR. DI FAZIO: Would Your Honours give me a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Whilst Mr. Di Fazio is checking his notes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- I wonder if I might ask whether he could establish from the witness how it was that the Albanians he says he was speaking to knew this information. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, perhaps if you put a bit more direct questions as: Did you learn it in a bar, in the village, wherever? MR. DI FAZIO: No, no, I think that's --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the question I was directing my comment to wasn't so much how this witness learnt, but how the people he was speaking to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I would like to have the whole picture, including more details about where and when. MR. DI FAZIO: Certainly, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Witness, you heard that exchange with Defence counsel and the Trial Chamber now and myself. Now, what we'd all like to know is a bit more about what -- about these bombs -- I'm sorry, the bags supposedly containing the bombs. And you've told us that -- so far that you were -- there weren't many Serbs in the area, so the people who told you were Albanians, and that it was -- you've also told us that it happened during informal conversations. Now, can you think back, please, and try and tell us if the -- where the informal conversations happened, whether they happened in a coffee shop, or in a bar, or in the street, or at a house of a friend? And secondly, secondly, and importantly, can you tell us if you know how they knew what was in the bags? So try and direct your mind back to those two matters and see if you can provide us with any more details; if you can't, say so. But if you do have any more details, please let us know.

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, may I ask you, nevertheless, to try hard. Was it when you visited people? Was it when you met people in the street that they told you about it? You said you asked for it. Were you confident to ask?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Given the fact that at the time they started pulling cars over at night, the police and that sort of thing, it was just loose talk, really, and I was involved. And I got to that particular question at one point. I don't remember who I asked the question specifically, but the answer I got at the time was just that. How did that person come to be familiar with that particular piece of information is really not something that I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do I understand from your answer that it was one person who told you, and not several persons who told you the same story?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: That would be one thing I would be interested in. Mr. Stojanovic, you mentioned that quite a few of the persons who came through Dubrava to the village of Gllogjan were not from the village, and, therefore, the question would have been interesting, I think, where they then went to. Because then you said, Well, they lived there, but according to your first information it's -- it appears to be also a crowd of people from somewhere else. And where they went to, do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know where they were on their way to, but again I must say many of the Albanians worked somewhere abroad. It's possible that those people were residents of Glodjane whose faces I have forgotten. There were people there who did not look familiar to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And just one last question on this topic. In answer to the President's question, you said that this piece of information about the bombs in the bags, in the Marlboro bags, occurred in the context of another conversation about loose talk about cars being pulled over at night. Can you tell us if you were given the information about the bags during some more general discussion about what was going on in your area? Do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't quite understand the question fully. If you could please run it past me again.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You said that you were engaged and there was some loose talk about the cars being pulled over, and that's when the topic of the young men and the bags turned -- arose. What I want to know is: Did you get the information about the young men and what was in the bags during a conversation about the general security situation in your area?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it was about the general security situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. You earlier mentioned in your evidence the Haradinaj house, which was I think - unless I'm wrong - I think you said quite close to your place. Did that place have a wall around it, the house? Did the Haradinaj house have a wall around it?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could you see into it from -- into the compound, into the yard, from your house?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: You could, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: So if one just stood on the ground, you could actually see inside?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: No, not inside. The wall kept us from seeing inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want you now again to keep your mind on the first three months of 1998. In that particular time, did you see any vehicular traffic, vehicles, around the Haradinaj compound?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: I did see vehicles bringing construction material, but I also spoke to a number of Albanians who told me that it wasn't just construction material, but beneath all those piles of stuff there were weapons concealed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And, again, can you remember which Albanians it was who provided you with this information?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: I don't remember. A lot of Albanians used to come to our place; therefore, it's difficult to remember who specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you ever see the number plates on the car -- on the vehicles?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Most of the times I didn't catch the plates, but normally those were cars belonging to Albanian companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, apart from seeing vehicles turn up with construction materials on it, and apart from being told on some occasion by some Albanian that there might have been weapons hidden underneath the construction materials, you have no other information about the topic. Do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, could you tell us was it one person who told you about these weapons? Were there more?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One, I think one, but I can't remember. It was just loose talk, and sometimes you came across subjects like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, what was your brother Predrag's job in the first few months of 1998? What was he -- what was his work?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Since the 1980s, my brother had been with the police in Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The information that you got about the young men carrying grenades in Marlboro bags and the possibility of weaponry being hidden in the construction materials of -- going to the Haradinaj compound, and people being pulled over at night, as you say, did you ever give your brother details of that, make any sort of report to him?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: No, never. I never really focused on that much. It was just loose talk.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: But what I want to know is this: Did you report it to him, either in a formal or informal way?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: No, or rather, I rarely even saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you report it in an informal or formal way to any other Serbian police force member, any other Serbian police officer?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: No. I had no time for things like those --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you --

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: -- nor would I ever normally be involved in anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Fair enough. Just listen to my question, sir, please. Did you report it in a formal or informal way to any member of the military, the Serb military?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you have any idea what Predrag's job in the police was in the first three months of 1998, what sort of work he did in the police?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was a beat copper.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And do you know where he was stationed?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: I know very, very little about his job.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you know where he was stationed in the first three months of 1998, where his beat was?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: In Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And in 1998, in the first three months, did you -- did you - you personally - or any other members of your family possess weapons that were kept at the house, at the house in Dubrava?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: I never did. The only thing there was in our house was a hunting rifle and my father's pistol. I don't think anyone else in our household actually had a weapon, not that I know of.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And do you know how long that hunting rifle and pistol had been in the possession of the family?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: I really don't know, believe me.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. I'll just persist a little more with that. Can you tell us if it was a matter of days, weeks, months, or years that those two weapons had been in the family?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: It was a matter of years. It was something that my family inherited from my father, who had held a valid licence for it. It was a licensed pistol.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. I now want you to focus more specifically in the month of March 1998, and, in particular, the period of time around the 23rd/24th of March, 1998. At that particular time, where were you spending your nights?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: As far as I can recall - and I don't really recall all that -- okay, yes, I do remember, I spent my nights at home.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did any -- I don't think it's in dispute. Was there a shoot-out of some sort at the Haradinaj compound around that date?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: I spent my nights at home, but in the morning I would go out, and then I think it seems to me that I came back for a short time, and when I did get back there was gun-fire around the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. So -- and do you remember the date? It doesn't matter if you don't, but if you -- if you can tell us the date that you're talking about when you came back and there was gun-fire around the house, tell us; if you're not sure, say so.

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Just the date or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, just the date.

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: The 24th of March, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, on that day did you go out on one of your work trips and leave the house?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: I think I did in the morning, but I can't be certain, and then after a while I returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And what did you notice when you returned?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: I noticed that there was some fighting around Ramush's house.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's obviously quite close to your house. What did you do when you saw what was going on?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: There were police around there, on the road, in my yard, and they ordered me to get in, get inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was your mother there?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you remember any other members of your family being present?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: There was my small nephew, a son of my brother Vlado, he was 3 years old at the time; and Dragoslav.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you have a chance to see what sort of weaponry was being used, either by the police or the people against whom they were directing their fire? What sort of weapons were being used?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: I don't know about weapons. There were some rifles. I don't know whether they were automatic rifles or some other kind, I really don't know, I really can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How many -- about how many police officers were on your land?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Maybe 15 or 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How did you even get close to your house in your car? How did you even get the car close to the house if there's all this shooting and policemen milling about the place?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Well, I had arrived from the direction of Babaloc, and there was no shooting in that area, in the area from which I had come in. There was fighting around the house and then in the direction of Glodjane.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. So you came in from Babaloc, which is to the south of Dubrava. So you didn't have to go through Glodjane to get to your house on that day. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you able to get the car -- your car close to the house and, obviously, get inside the house without any problems?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: No, there were problems. I had to ask a couple of police officers standing there in the very centre of Dubrava to let me through.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And once you made it to your house and laid eyes on your nephew and your mother and brother and were told to get inside, did you remain inside the house?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, for most of the time; 80 per cent of the time I was inside the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And did fighting continue that day?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, all the way until the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: So fighting continued for a matter of several hours at least; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, several hours. But it moved away from the -- the fighting moved away from Ramush's house. At the time when I arrived, the fighting was there; and then it moved towards the village of Glodjane because the police were trying to pull out a police officer who had been wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thinking back now, when you first arrived, there was -- fighting was already underway; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Fighting was already underway with police officers stationed or positioned around the area, but also on your land; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, one part of our property --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yeah, okay --

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: But mostly --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. Fine. And fighting continued with police officers in the area -- in the immediate area firing and also from your land firing; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Eventually the focus of the fighting shifted away from the Haradinaj --

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: -- compound and moved off -- and went -- and made its way towards Glodjane from what you could discern anyway; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, yes, where I was already able to see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters apologise, the witness is not speaking very loudly and sometimes it's difficult to understand him. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, try not to mumble and speak clearly and a little bit more loudly, if you wouldn't mind, so the interpreters can hear you. We want to be able to hear what your -- we want to be able to hear what you say. Okay? What I want to know is this: When you got back the fighting was already underway and it took some time for the fighting to move from the Haradinaj compound off towards Glodjane. That is so, isn't it, from what you said?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: About how long would you say it took for the fighting to move away from the Haradinaj compound towards wherever, Glodjane?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was it a matter of minutes or some longer time?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: I really can't remember. I think maybe several minutes, but I don't really remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. And one thing is for sure, it continued for many hours until the evening?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And they were engaged in this fighting at least I think 15 or 20 policemen who -- located on your land alone; correct?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Not all of them were on our land. Some of them walked down the road, some of them were located in a corner of our property, they were hiding behind some bushes and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Large numbers of policemen would you say?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: What do you mean large number of policemen? I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Figures well beyond -- beyond the 20 or so that were on your land?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Well, there were that many policemen on our land, that's the number that I was able to see and I didn't see the rest. I know that there were some on the road and in the corner of our property. That would be the number of police officers that I actually was able to see, around 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. Anyway, it took these numbers of policemen -- well, I'll withdraw that. The police did not appear to have, from what you could see and observe, anything described as a swift victory that day, from what you could see and observe at least?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. You -- did you stay in the area following this shoot-out?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. And one other question is: Did you see the police employing helicopters and rocket-launchers?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, I did see helicopters. I didn't see any rocket-launchers. I saw that some helicopters had been trying to land to get the wounded police officer, Otovic, out, to land there, but they failed to do so a number of times.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Have you got any idea what was preventing the helicopters from landing and getting the police officer out?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Well, fire was opened on them from Ramush Haradinaj's house, so they couldn't approach that spot at all. They couldn't get the wounded police officer out.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And casualties from this encounter, were you -- you've already mentioned one, and that's the police officer. Did you become aware or were you aware of any Albanian casualties, casualties from the other side, that -- the men that the police were fighting, or indeed anyone else, civilians, for that matter?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: No, I didn't know at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What about afterwards, did you find out afterwards?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: The next day I read in "Zeri Rinis" and "Rilindja," I learned that two young men also were casualties.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: I don't know whether this was as a result of this action or whether this was someplace else.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you and your family leave your property that day or the next day?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: No, we left that evening. A police officer came and ordered us to leave our property for security reasons. We had to leave our house.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And where did you go?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Dragoslav and my mother went to Djakovica to make a statement, and I went to Erec, and then I went to my brother's place in Decani.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And where did you continue -- where did you personally - I'm not talking about your siblings - but where did you live in the period of time -- in the -- for the remainder of March and the first two weeks of April?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: After a short while, maybe two or three days, my mother, myself, Dragoslav were given accommodation in a camp in Decani. The municipality provided us with this accommodation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What sort of camp is this?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Well, it was used as a summer resort camp by some companies, but now it was run-down.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is there a monastery near it?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, the Decani monastery.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And was this place -- has it got bungalow -- bungalow-type accommodation?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, yes, bungalows.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And when you went to -- when you and your brother and your mother went to live there, who else was there?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: At that time we did not encounter anyone there, but afterwards other civilians came in, civilians who had had to leave their villages for security reasons, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What ethnicity were these villagers?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: All of them Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And what villages are we talking about, what area?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: The Decani area, Dasinovac, Ratis, and the villages up there where there had been some Serbs still living there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. Just to -- I just want -- if you can do this, please do. I want you to give us a list of villages -- I want you to give -- thinking back at the people who were there who came to this camp, which villages they came from. Now, you've already mentioned the Decani area, that's an area, but you've mentioned specifically Dasinovac and Ratis. Are you aware of this camp containing or accommodating Serbs from other villages other than Dasinovac and Ratis? Can you remember any other Serbs from other villages; and if you know the names of the villages, I want to hear them?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Ljubarda. Well, I don't know where the other Serbs had come from, but mostly from this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And did you continue to live there for some weeks?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: I live -- or we lived there for almost a year, but I was on the move all the time. I was going to Belgrade, all over Kosovo, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: In the -- sorry?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: But my mother was there all this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, in the height of summer of that year, 1998, about how many Serbs would you say had appeared in this camp?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Some 30 families or so, maybe more, but I'm sure that there were 30 or so.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And can you tell the Trial Chamber if they all came from the area -- from your area or whether they came from further afield, from other parts of Kosovo or other parts of --

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: No, only from the municipality of Decani.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. And 30 families, what does that translate to in terms of individual people, approximately, of course?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Well, I really can't tell. Three, four, maybe even more members per family. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to now ask you a little bit about your property. How long had your house and land been with you in your family?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Well, since 1922, as far as I can remember; this is how long my family owned this property.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Do you still own it?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: When was the last time that you went back to it?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: I was there when the OSCE came to Kosovo, and that was the last time. I never went back.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you give us a time on that, please?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Well, it was in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Your Honours, it's only 22 minutes past, but this would be a natural break because I'm going to get on to other events that -- I'm happy to go on if you prefer, but if it's convenient this would make a more natural time for us to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I've got one question: How much time do you think you would need, Mr. Di Fazio? MR. DI FAZIO: 40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 40 minutes. Yes. We'll then have an early break. We will resume at ten minutes to 11.00, but before we adjourn I would like to briefly deal with the parties with the exhibits of the last witness. So, Madam Usher -- We'll have a break, Mr. Stojanovic. Would you please follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, I don't know whether you are in a position to deal with the exhibits for the last witness P31, map marked, any objections? No, it is admitted into evidence. P32, the photograph shown of the village of Glodjane. No objections; admitted into evidence. P33, release sheet of the hospital, no objection; admitted into evidence. P34, video-clip; admitted into evidence since I see the Defence nodding that there are no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just for your information, the -- it's, as a matter of fact, it's the transcript that is a -- is an e-court document, but it refers to a DVD which is in the hands of the registry. P35, aerial photograph of Glodjane and surroundings, no objection; admitted into evidence. P36, photograph showing the house of Ramush Haradinaj, that's admitted into evidence. Then we move on to the Defence exhibits. I'd like to know whether they will be tendered because -- D22, OTP witness statement of Dragoslav Stojanovic, 2001, is that tendered, Mr. Emmerson?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I think I dealt with it in cross-examination, Your Honour, so I'm happy to leave it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then it remains marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Not tendered, therefore no admission. D23, Humanitarian Law Centre incident report dated 9th of April, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: That is already -- I think that is already an exhibit; if it isn't, then it's tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think as a -- we'll have to check that whether we have that because some of them -- yes. Okay. Any objection? We'll check whether it's -- Mr. Di Fazio, D23, Humanitarian Law Centre report -- MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was part of the material that was introduced by Witness Andjelkovic, if I -- MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, is that the -- is that the report dealing with the words of the mother or the --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: That's exactly what I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think it -- well, we have two, as a matter of fact, because D26, I think, as a matter of fact is -- one will be the mother, the other one will be the brother because they both deal with events -- both reports are dated the 9th of February. The one is -- D23 is 65 ter 1161; whereas, D26 is 1162. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, I could -- could I speak to Mr. Re before I give any indication? I think it's probably going to be no problem at all, but I would just like to check with him before I say anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: The position is, Your Honour, is that those exhibits - I will be corrected if I'm wrong - were part originally of a collective exhibit tendered by the Prosecution through Marijana Andjelkovic. Now, it wasn't part of the notebook, the translation of which is still to be finalised, but certainly that, as I understand it, is the position. D23 is, indeed, the mother, Ljubica's, report of the 9th of April, and D26 is the brother Vladimir report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: And both are tendered, so far as the Defence are concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: For the purposes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll hear from the Prosecution whether there's any objection, but at the same time we'll take the effort to check whether these are already part of the collective. Because then it -- perhaps it would be better to -- we have the specific numbering of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: eglodj.doc.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: eglodj.doc. And we'll check there whether they are already in evidence. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Can I indicate as a matter of practicality why I separated them out in this way. It's simply that given the pressure of time in the course of the examination of witnesses, it takes such a long time for things to be loaded up and searched through. It seems simpler --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: -- when those individual documents, where they're being focused on, to be separately exhibited from the collective batch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we have the next one is D24. Let me just have a look at what that was. Document ID was ID 020733, Mr. Emmerson. I've got no description on my list at this moment. Madam Registrar, is there -- I could try to find it. Yes, D24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the aerial photograph --

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Aerial photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, aerial photograph. No objection, Mr. Di Fazio? MR. DI FAZIO: None, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then D24 is admitted into evidence. The 25 press articles Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Yes, I will tender that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Di Fazio? MR. DI FAZIO: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then D25 is admitted into evidence. We will resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, please proceed. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honours. Before I proceed, if it's any assistance to you, those other two documents that were not fully admitted into evidence before the break, I can indicate to you that there's no problem with those going fully into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: These are the two Humanitarian Law Centre Institute reports? MR. DI FAZIO: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So D23 and D26 admitted into evidence under the proviso that even if they are in evidence, perhaps keep it as it is. It's just one page. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: We've checked the position. They are, in fact, part of Exhibit P5, but I hope Your Honours will forgive me, when particular reports --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: They have them done double and now in isolated format in evidence as well. Please proceed. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, you've told us all about the shoot-out at the Haradinaj compound and how you took up residence in this camp. Following that, did you return to your home in April?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Not as far as I remember. No. I'm certain that it wasn't in April.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. Did you go back to your home at all following your going to -- moving to the camp in Decani?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: I said a while ago that I had returned there only for as long as the OSCE mission was still around.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Were you ever assaulted or attacked personally, physically, in 1998?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: On the 18th of April, 1998 -- I'm sorry, I misunderstood your question the first time around. Back in 1998 on the 18th of April, my brothers Dragoslav and Vesko and I set out to get something from Dubrava.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, did you make it to Dubrava?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, we did. We drove through Babaloc and drove all the way to the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I want to know who precisely went to Dubrava. You were there; your brother, Dragoslav was there; and the third person, who was that, who was the third person?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Vesko Stijovic; Veselin Stijovic called Vesko.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, he's not your brother, is he?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: He's our cousin, which I believe is the word you use around these parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Right. Okay. Fine. Anyway, you went and did you travel there in the cars that you had mentioned earlier in your evidence, in the Mazda and the Lada?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes. I drove the Lada, and Dragoslav drove the Mazda.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And what was the reason you went back to your home?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: We had fled to the camp in Decani, and we didn't have our own things with us, so we drove back to our home to get some things, some personal belongings, and also to get some hay for the livestock that we had previously taken to the monastery in Decani, our own livestock.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And did you have a trailer to load the hay into?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, Dragoslav had a trailer, the kind normally used to tow cars, but we used it for taking all this hay from one place to the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: About what time of day did you get there?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Between half past 8.00 and 9.00, at least as far as I can remember. I'm not certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Is this half past 8.00 or 9.00 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, thank you for that clarification, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you start to load up the trailer and the car -- the cars?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes -- no, not the trailer. We loaded stuff into the Lada, Vesko and I did. Dragoslav was trying to fix the trailer. One of the tires was flat and it needed changing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in your own words, can you tell us what happened next?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: After a brief while, having loaded all the things into the Lada, we heard a shot from Dubrava. We didn't really pay attention to that initial shot; however, this one was soon followed by other shots from Glodjane, more specifically from the direction of Ramush Haradinaj's house. I was standing in the doorway of my house, and then I took cover inside. As far as I can remember, Dragoslav and Veselin dashed straight into the house. Dragoslav did, and I'm not sure about Veselin. After that, the shooting went on for about 40 minutes until they arrived in the front yard, at which point we were ordered to open the door. Dragoslav did, he spoke back to them, and he opened the door. And then between 15, 20, or 30 --

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you. I just wanted to be clear about one thing. Did the shooting go on for 40 or 14 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: At least as far as I can now remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thanks. And just while we're on this, the shooting, as far as you can tell, was it small-arms fire? By that, I mean rifles or automatic rifles, or was there other weaponry used, as far as you're aware?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: I think automatic weapons and small-arms fire for the most part.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And do you know if your house was damaged?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: The window-panes were smashed and the Lada was damaged. It was parked just in front of the Mazda, and it was damaged on all sides. Bullets had ricochetted through the windows and into the rooms.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And how did you protect yourself?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Well, given the fact that there is a corridor there and doors leading into all the rooms, we for the most part took cover in that hallway, corridor. And while the attacks continued, Dragoslav every once in a while looked to the window. To the extent that he could, he would pop up to see what was going on outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you just tell us this: Were any of you three men - you, Dragoslav, or your cousin - armed?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: None of us were, not before, not now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. Right. Thank you. And you had got to your point in your narrative before where you said that -- I'm not sure, a number of men appeared or came to the house. Just continue from there and give us details of about how many men appeared at the house, and I'd also like to know how they were dressed and whether they were armed.

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: They were dressed in camouflage uniform and armed with small arms. Their uniforms were camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did all of the men have camouflage uniforms and were the uniforms complete; that is, in the sense from neck to -- neck to toe in camouflage or were they partially camouflaged?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: No, not all did. There were soldiers who had the camouflage tops, and the bottoms were just jeans or other kind of civilian clothes, or the other way around. So it was a mixed bag, you might say.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And did they have any insignia on them that you can recall?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: As far as I remember, they had the Kosovo Liberation Army insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Could we show the witness P9, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio, wouldn't it be a better idea first to ask the witness whether he could describe such an item, and then -- MR. DI FAZIO: That's a good idea. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO:

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: You heard His Honour's question. What did it look like before we show you anything?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: On the outside it was red, and inside there was a double-headed eagle and then "UCK," which stands for Kosovo Liberation Army underneath in yellow letters.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thanks. Okay. Can you have a look at this thing that will come up on your screen, please. Have you seen that before, that symbol?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes, I saw it the moment they captured us. I hadn't seen it before then.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: I'm done with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you recognise any of the men who came in -- who were at your house on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: The first to come in through the veranda door was Ramush's brother Daut, who was then followed by Xhavit Nimonaj. I recognised quite many of them, but we were soon ordered to lie down and to lie face down. When we lay down on the floor, they started beating us, me and Veselin. Dragoslav was hit by Daut with a rifle-butt on the way in already, and they started beating us and verbally abusing us.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you remember what they were saying to you in terms of verbal abuse? Can you remember the actual -- the actual words?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Normally, it was about our Serb mothers and other derogatory terms like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Was there reference in the course of the abuse to your ethnicity, to the fact that you were Serbs, apart from reference to your Serb mothers?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. The -- you've already told us about Daut Haradinaj, but this other fellow Xhavit Nimonaj, where was he from?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: One of our neighbours, our left-hand neighbour, when looking from Dubrava to Glodjane. Same distance as Ramush.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And had he been a neighbour of yours for many years?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. How long were you in the house before you were taken away?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Very briefly. I can't be more specific, but very briefly, and then we were taken outside to the front yard. They ID'd us and told us to keep our heads down, to not look them in the face. And they asked me and Veselin to produce our IDs, which we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Why -- what about Dragoslav, was he asked to produce ID or not?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: I don't remember. In the meantime, Nasim Haradinaj had arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And who is Nasim Haradinaj?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Nasim Haradinaj is Ramush Haradinaj's cousin.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And had you known him for a number of years from the local area?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you. You've described some of the verbal abuse and Dragoslav being hit by the rifle-butt by Daut Haradinaj. In the house, how -- what -- did you and Veselin also receive any beating?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes. We were lying face-down, so I couldn't see who it was beating me and hitting me with rifle-butts and kicking me. I really couldn't see who it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Okay. At this juncture, at this point where you had been beaten and the three of you are outside and you're being told to produce ID and then -- and then keep your heads down, could you tell if any of you, any of you three, were -- had any visible signs of injury; in other words, if there was blood on any of you at that point?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Not at that point. I wasn't really looking. We weren't able to even look at each other, since we'd been told to keep our heads down.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right. And where did you go from there?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Well, after a while, I'm not sure how long, they started taking us to the Glodjane HQ, or at least that's what they said.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And where did you actually end up?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: We went to Smajl Haradinaj's house. He is the father of Nasim Haradinaj. On our way there, they kept verbally abusing us and hitting us and firing bullets behind us and just past our heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you walk there?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now, think back on the trip from your place to Smajl Haradinaj's house. On the way, on the way from your place to Smajl Haradinaj's house, did you recognise anyone?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: At one point I did on the way to the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Ramush Haradinaj near the front yard. There is a small path forking off in the direction of his house, and I recognised many of my neighbours who were involved in the whole process; but they kept telling us to not look left and right but just to keep our heads down.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Now where -- you say you recognised Ramush Haradinaj near the front yard. Where was he located, the front yard of whose house?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: No, he was outside the front yard of the house on that path- what should I call it? - I'm not sure if I can clarify that any further. There was a meadow and a small path leading to his house.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: To the Haradinaj compound, the one that you described earlier; is that the place?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And was he alone when you saw him or was he in company with other people?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: As far as I remember, there were two or three other persons, two of them standing there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And what sort of clothing did he have on when you saw him?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Green camouflage and a red beret.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: A what? A red beret?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: Black, black, I'm sorry, black, black beret.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And about how far from Smajl Haradinaj's house is -- was this place that you saw him?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: 700 to 800 metres, not more.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: All right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Did we understand correctly 700 to 800 metres, not more?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Between his house and Smajl's house.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you. MR. DI FAZIO: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And you were taken to Smajl Haradinaj's house, and where in the place were you taken to?

utterances.speaker: MIJAT STOJANOVIC.
utterances.text: We were taken to his house, which had stood empty for quite some time because Smajl Haradinaj's family were not staying in Glodjane up until several days before. They had been somewhere abroad. As far as I know, they had been in Sweden. Again, we were taken to the first floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
